subtype: Approach: sets a device so strict that it backfires [Pitfall]
passage:
Friday, 9:30 pm. Well, that plan is dead. On Monday I set a blocker to lock every app on my phone, all day, no exceptions. No messages, no maps, no bank. I thought: cold turkey, total focus. Today at eleven, Ishita sent a photo of the client's signed form on the work chat and asked me to forward it within ten minutes. My phone would not open the chat. I hunted for a way round it, panicked, deleted the blocker altogether, and still sent the form twenty minutes late. Now everything is open again and I scrolled for an hour tonight. The rule was too strict. It never made room for the one app I actually need.

Naveen

qa.a: Ishita asked Naveen to forward the client's signed form within ten minutes.

qa.a: Naveen feels frustrated and a little defeated, calling the plan dead.

qa.q: What could Naveen do differently next time?
qa.a: Naveen could set a lighter lock that blocks only the distracting apps and keeps the work chat open.

qa.q: How might Ishita have felt while waiting for the form?
qa.a: Ishita may have felt anxious about the deadline and puzzled about why Naveen was unreachable.

grounding: Shows Naveen locking all apps for a day, breaking the lock in a hurry when work needs one and dropping the system.

Monday, 9:02 am

Shankar: Big day. I've locked every app on my phone till 8 pm. No chat, no email, nothing. Total focus 💪
Gurpreet: Every app? Even work chat?
Shankar: Especially that. Distraction machine.
Gurpreet: Hmm. What if the client calls?
Shankar: They'll wait.

11:47 am

Shankar: Help. Client needs the file NOW and it's only on work chat. The lock needs a 10-minute wait to unlock.
Gurpreet: Uh oh.
Shankar: Couldn't wait. Uninstalled the lock app. Sent the file. They were already annoyed.
Gurpreet: So back to the plan tomorrow?
Shankar: Forget it. Clearly doesn't work for me.
Gurpreet: Maybe the plan just needed a gap for work stuff?
Shankar: Maybe. Not today.

qa.q: What time did Shankar lock the apps until?

qa.a: Shankar was panicked and frustrated because the client needed the file and the lock forced a wait.

qa.q: What would you change first about Shankar's plan?
qa.a: Allow work chat during office hours and lock only the distracting apps, so the device doesn't block real work.

qa.q: How might the client have seen the delay?
qa.a: The client was already annoyed, probably feeling Shankar was slow or hard to reach.

grounding: A worker locks every app for the day, needs one for work, breaks the lock in a hurry and gives up the system.

subtype: Approach: sets a device so strict that it backfires [Pitfall]
passage: Arnab ran the accounts for a small seed shop in the market town of Bolpur. After weeks of losing evenings to his phone, he installed a strict blocker on Monday morning: every app locked until 9 pm. He felt proud as he slid the phone into his pocket. At noon a farmer came to pay for seed bags and wanted to pay through the phone. Himani, the owner, called out, "Arnab, check if the money's come." He couldn't open anything. The farmer waited, frowning. Arnab fumbled with the blocker's settings, deleted it in a panic and finally checked. That night he didn't reinstall it. "It's useless," he told Himani. "Too much trouble." His evenings went back to scrolling.

qa.q: What time did Arnab's blocker keep apps locked until?
How did Arnab feel while the farmer waited?
qa.a: He felt flustered and embarrassed, fumbling with the settings in front of the farmer and Himani.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could fix it?
qa.a: The blocker covered even the payment app his job needs; blocking only the apps that ate his evenings would keep work possible.

qa.q: How did Himani experience the moment?
qa.a: Himani was probably annoyed and puzzled that a simple payment check held up a customer.

grounding: A worker's all-day app lock blocks a work need, so he breaks it in a hurry and abandons the whole system.
